Many small purchases, a few large purchases: payment counts and dollar shares

Five charts compare 2025 Bank of Canada purchase-count and dollar shares with an independent purchase tally. See category changes, average tickets and undefined zero-total shares.

By TickerLantern Research · Published 25 October 2026 · 7 min read
Sources reviewed 25 October 2026

Change an assumption. Follow the result.

Count purchases and purchase dollars in one invented tally

The first two figures use fixed 2025 Bank of Canada consumer-purchase payment shares, reviewed 25 October 2026; report metadata is dated August 2026. The nine published payment bins are retained. The second figure explicitly combines three credit bins and three debit bins for a one-year calculation; standalone Credit/Debit in the first figure are not those combined totals. The 2025 categories cannot be fully harmonized with earlier years. Source rounding is preserved, with count shares summing to 100.0% and value shares to 100.1%; no normalization or personal probability is inferred. The final three figures are a separate invented purchase tally, not a reconstruction of the survey. Each purchase has one method; assumed mean final prices include applicable taxes and are rounded to cents. There are no refunds, fees, split tenders or currency conversions. Counts are whole numbers. Count shares require a positive total count; dollar shares require positive total dollars. Empty distributions display an empty ring and unavailable shares. An entered ticket for a method with no purchases contributes no dollars. The tally calculates no income, available cash, card repayment, interest, rewards, merchant acceptance, outage or fraud risk. A credit purchase is counted once at purchase; later settlement is a separate cash-flow question.

The central idea

A purchase counts once but can carry many dollars. Before reading a payment-method percentage as a spending pattern, identify whether its denominator is transactions, dollars or people.

01

Count the purchases and then count their dollars

Suppose a purchase list contains six small cash purchases, three debit purchases and one larger credit purchase. A count-based chart gives every purchase one unit. A dollar-based chart instead weights each purchase by its amount. The same list can therefore have very different method shares without any arithmetic error.

For a defined tally, purchase-count share is a method’s count divided by the total number of purchases. Purchase-dollar share is its spending divided by total spending. Neither denominator is income, the number of people holding a card or the amount of money currently available in a bank account.

The first two charts use fixed official 2025 observations. The last three use an independently invented tally that the controls can change. The example explains the denominator arithmetic; it does not estimate how an individual should pay or reconstruct the survey from three personal categories.

02

Read the nine published 2025 reporting categories together

The Bank of Canada’s Methods-of-Payment Survey dashboard describes consumer purchases, using a questionnaire and a three-day payment diary. Its 2025 data are accompanied by report metadata dated August 2026. This article reviewed the dashboard and data on 25 October 2026.

The paired chart retains all nine current reporting bins. In particular, the standalone labels Credit and Debit sit alongside separately reported contactless categories. Reading Credit’s 14.2% count share as all credit-card use would omit the other credit bins.

Published count shares sum to 100.0%; dollar shares sum to 100.1% at the source precision. The table preserves those values instead of changing Other or normalizing every row. These are purchase measures, not a census of every transfer and payment in the economy. The data extract supplies no confidence intervals, so none are invented here.

03

Keep the 2025 classification break visible

The dashboard notes a reporting change in 2025. Contactless card payments now distinguish physical cards from cards linked to mobile devices, and the Mobile app category excludes those mobile contactless card purchases. The Bank states that the 2025 categories cannot be fully harmonized with previous survey years.

These charts therefore compare categories within 2025. A smooth Mobile app line across the classification change could mix a measurement change with behaviour. Historical blanks in newly introduced categories should also not be replaced with fabricated zeros.

The second chart makes a disclosed one-year combination: Credit, Contactless credit and Contactless credit, mobile form the three-credit-bin group; the corresponding debit bins form another. Cash, Mobile app and Other stay separate. This grouping is explicit and does not silently redefine the labels in the original nine-row chart.

04

A difference in percentage points is a denominator comparison

In the three combined credit bins, the 2025 count share is 48.2% and the dollar share is 58.5%. Subtracting count share from dollar share gives positive 10.3 percentage points. Cash goes the other way: 9.6% of dollars minus 17.9% of count gives negative 8.3 points.

The signed bars display that subtraction. A positive value means the group has a larger share of dollars than purchases; negative means a smaller share. These are neither annual investment returns nor changes from a previous year. A gap of 10.3 percentage points is also different from saying a quantity grew by 10.3%.

Different purchase sizes can produce such a pattern, as the invented tally demonstrates. The public shares alone do not identify why payment methods and amounts are associated. They do not establish that choosing a card causes higher spending or that a reader will face an equivalent distribution.

The five gaps sum to 0.1 point because source dollar shares total 100.1% and count shares total 100.0%. That small residual is retained as a rounding consequence. It is not treated as missing income or a new payment category.

05

Reconcile the invented ten-purchase example

The default tally has six cash purchases at a mean CAD 5, three debit purchases at a mean CAD 40 and one credit purchase at CAD 350. The means are assumed final purchase amounts including applicable taxes. Each purchase belongs to exactly one of the three teaching categories, with no split tender, refund or currency conversion.

Method dollars are CAD 30, CAD 120 and CAD 350. Total count is ten and total dollars are CAD 500. The count ring therefore shows 60%, 30% and 10%, while the dollar ring shows 6%, 24% and 70%. One purchase can be only one tenth of the count while carrying seven tenths of the cost.

The waterfall reconciles those method dollars to CAD 500. Dividing by ten gives a mean purchase amount of CAD 50. That mean does not identify the median purchase or the distribution within each payment category; the tool knows only counts and assumed category means.

The toy’s three broad labels are separate from the Bank’s nine reporting bins. Its 60% cash count share is an invented result, not a competing estimate of the official 2025 cash share. Source figures remain fixed when a toy count or price changes.

06

Change the amount without changing the number of purchases

Keep the default counts and raise only the credit mean ticket from CAD 350 to CAD 700. There are still ten purchases, including exactly one credit purchase. The credit count share remains 10%, but total spending rises to CAD 850.

The credit dollar share becomes CAD 700 ÷ CAD 850, or about 82.35%. Overall mean purchase amount rises from CAD 50 to CAD 85. The unchanged count ring, changed dollar ring and larger waterfall endpoint show why the same transaction frequency can coexist with very different spending.

This comparison changes a price assumption, rather than measuring the effect of switching payment methods. Relabeling the same completed purchases while preserving all final prices leaves total spending unchanged. A real discount, surcharge, interest cost or reward would need its own cash treatment; none is automatically inserted into this tally.

The entered average ticket for a method with zero purchases has no effect on its contribution to dollars. It is an unused assumption, not an observed purchase mean. This distinction becomes useful when comparing a rarely used method with a frequently used one.

07

Keep zero purchases distinct from zero purchase dollars

If all three counts are zero, total purchases and dollars are zero. Both share distributions are undefined because their denominators are zero. The rings are empty and label their shares unavailable. Three 0% shares would not form a meaningful distribution of purchases.

A different case has positive counts but zero prices. Count shares remain defined, while dollar shares are undefined because total dollars are zero. Overall mean purchase amount is zero in that case, because zero dollars are divided by a positive count. With no purchases at all, the overall mean is unavailable.

The controls require whole nonnegative counts and nonnegative assumed prices. Cash amounts are rounded to cents before multiplication. A negative purchase amount would represent a refund or another transaction type, which is outside this small model rather than silently mixed into a positive-purchase distribution.

The distinction is mathematical, not an assessment of whether a zero-price transaction belongs in the actual survey. The official dataset follows its own transaction definitions; the teaching tally simply makes its assumptions explicit.

08

Bring the purchase tally into a separate funding calendar

Purchase dollars measure what the invented list costs. They do not show the income that funds it, when cash leaves a bank account or whether a credit-card balance is paid in full. A method share cannot establish affordability, card interest, unused credit or an emergency reserve.

For a budget that recognizes spending when a purchase occurs, a later card payment settles that obligation rather than creating the same consumption expense again. The purchase-and-repayment ledger guide develops that distinction. A separate cash calendar still needs the settlement date and actual amount. Keep those two views consistent instead of adding the purchase and its settlement as two copies of the same spending.

This article calculates no rewards, repayment schedule, merchant acceptance, fraud probability or outage risk. Those questions require their own definitions and evidence. The narrow result here is inspectable: counts reconcile to total purchases, method dollars reconcile to spending, and each share states the denominator it uses.

Sources and scope

Public sources reviewed on 25 October 2026. Charts labelled “Official statistics” or “Derived from official statistics” identify their source periods. Other charts are hypothetical scenarios. Original scenario calculations and research checklists are TickerLantern’s educational analysis; attributed publisher examples retain their stated source and scope.
